content: Ovulation induction using follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) is considered a second-line treatment for women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) who fail to ovulate or conceive after treatment with clomiphene citrate. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of gonadotrophins as a second-line therapy in women with clomiphene citrate-resistant PCOS or those who did not achieve ovulation or conception with clomiphene citrate. A comprehensive search was conducted in January 2018 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and others, to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The inclusion criteria focused on RCTs that reported clinical outcomes in women with PCOS undergoing ovulation induction with gonadotrophins, such as urinary-derived gonadotrophins (urofollitropin in purified or highly purified forms), human menopausal gonadotropin (HMG), highly purified HMG (HP-HMG), or recombinant FSH (rFSH). Trials involving co-treatment with other agents like clomiphene citrate, metformin, luteinizing hormone, or letrozole were excluded. The primary outcomes assessed were live birth rate and multiple pregnancy rate per woman. Secondary outcomes included clinical pregnancy rate, miscarriage rate, incidence of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), total gonadotrophin dose, and duration of stimulation. Data were analyzed using a fixed-effect model, and the quality of evidence was graded using GRADE criteria. Fifteen trials involving 2,387 women were included in the review. Ten trials compared recombinant FSH (rFSH) with urinary-derived gonadotrophins, while four trials compared purified FSH (FSH-P) with HMG. One trial compared FSH with continued clomiphene citrate. No trials directly compared highly purified FSH (FSH-HP) with FSH-P. Recombinant FSH (rFSH) versus urinary-derived gonadotrophins: There was low-quality evidence suggesting little or no difference in live birth rates between rFSH and urinary-derived gonadotrophins (risk ratio [RR] 1.21, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.83 to 1.78). For women with an average live birth rate of 16% using urinary-derived FSH, the live birth rate with rFSH was estimated to range between 13% and 28%. There was also low-quality evidence indicating little or no difference in the incidence of multiple pregnancies (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.61), clinical pregnancy rates (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.27), or miscarriage rates (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.71 to 2.04). The evidence was very low quality regarding whether rFSH reduces the incidence of OHSS (RR 1.48, 95% CI 0.82 to 2.65). Human menopausal gonadotrophin (HMG) or HP-HMG versus urinary FSH (uFSH): The evidence was very low quality and inconclusive regarding whether HMG or HP-HMG improves live birth rates compared to uFSH (RR 1.28, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.52). Similarly, there was very low-quality evidence regarding the effect of HMG or HP-HMG on multiple pregnancy rates (RR 2.13, 95% CI 0.51 to 8.91), clinical pregnancy rates (RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.66 to 2.59), miscarriage rates (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.97), or the incidence of OHSS (RR 7.07, 95% CI 0.42 to 117.81). Gonadotrophins versus continued clomiphene citrate: Gonadotrophins were associated with a higher live birth rate compared to continued clomiphene citrate (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.46; moderate-quality evidence). For women with a live birth rate of 41% using clomiphene citrate, the live birth rate with gonadotrophins was estimated to range between 43% and 60%. There was probably little or no difference in the incidence of multiple pregnancies between the two treatments (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.33 to 2.44; moderate-quality evidence). Gonadotrophins resulted in more clinical pregnancies (RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.52) but also more miscarriages (RR 2.23, 95% CI 1.11 to 4.47) compared to continued clomiphene citrate. None of the women in this comparison developed OHSS. Conclusions: There may be little or no difference in live birth rates, multiple pregnancy rates, clinical pregnancy rates, or miscarriage rates between urinary-derived gonadotrophins and recombinant FSH in women with PCOS. The evidence is uncertain regarding whether HMG or HP-HMG is superior or inferior to uFSH in terms of live birth rates, multiple pregnancy rates, clinical pregnancy rates, miscarriage rates, or the incidence of OHSS. In women who fail to conceive with clomiphene citrate, gonadotrophins appear to result in more live births compared to continued clomiphene citrate, without increasing the risk of multiple pregnancies. Cost and convenience should be considered when choosing between different gonadotrophin preparations.
